clue.text: Retired doctor introducing new deal to asylum

indicators.note: the doctor brings the new deal in, putting it between his own letters
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the doctor's letters are read in reverse

parts.note: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

indicators.note: new signals that the word deal is remade in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A doctor in retirement brings a new arrangement to a mental hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' turns the doctor into BM and 'new' makes EDLA; 'introducing' sets EDLA between B and M. Bedlam was London's Bethlem hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam was the popular name of Bethlem Royal Hospital, a London lunatic asylum, and the word came to mean any madhouse.

parts.note: a person carrying fourteen pounds too much seems meant, but this is a stone that is simply very heavy

explanation.walkthrough: A stone is also a British unit of body weight, fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A boulder is a large rock, a stone of great weight.

clue.text: Finished with church, we hear — will he ever learn?

indicators.note: we hear says the letters are spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: finished means done, and CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone through with churchgoing asks whether a slow pupil will ever learn.
explanation.walkthrough: DONE plus CE (Church of England), said aloud, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunce is a slow learner, the pupil about whom one asks despairingly if he will ever learn.

definitions.meaning: to direct, as when ... a letter or remarks to someone
a formal speech given to an audience

explanation.definitionFit: To address remarks is to direct them at someone, and an address is a formal speech.

indicators.note: to baffle is to confuse, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A tall story told to bewilder a legal man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baffle' rearranges the six letters of YARN and TO.
explanation.definitionFit: A notary is a legal official who certifies documents, a kind of lawyer.

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O
clock is slang for a person's face

explanation.surface: A timepiece shows the hour on its circular dial.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a person's face is their 'clock'.
explanation.definitionFit: O'clock is used in stating the time by the hour, as in three o'clock.

parts.note: bit rate reads whimsically as a rate of pay per bit, that is piecework

explanation.surface: Decide whether one has a right to be paid by the piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piecework' is pay by the item, so a BIT RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To arbitrate is to settle or determine a dispute as an impartial judge.

indicators.note: fever suggests agitation or delirium, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A face covering against hay fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fever' rearranges MASK and HAY; the whole clue also describes the veil.
explanation.definitionFit: A yashmak is the veil worn by some Muslim women, covering the face like a mask.

parts.note: a US President named for a shrub sending messages by wire seems meant; it is the informal spread of news by word of mouth

explanation.walkthrough: Two US Presidents were named Bush; intelligence here means news.
explanation.definitionFit: The bush telegraph is the rapid informal spreading of rumour and gossip, like a grapevine.

indicators.note: losing its head means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: Bruin is the traditional storybook name for a bear

explanation.surface: A bear loses its head among the wreckage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' removes the B from BRUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin, as in the ruins of a building, is what is left after destruction: wreckage.

parts.note: a double measure of Bass, the British beer, would be a big drink; read again, it is the bowed instrument whose notes are the lowest of the strings

explanation.walkthrough: Bass is a well-known British brand of beer; a 'double' is a large measure of a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest bowed string instrument plays very low notes, and its name also reads as a double measure of beer.

definitions.meaning: cleave can mean to cling to, the opposite of its splitting sense
to stick is to cling or remain attached

explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling fast, which is one sense of cleave and the everyday sense of stick.

clue.text: Tom has to order a little bull for sacrifice

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, a he-cat
OM is the Order of Merit

indicators.note: a little of the word bull is just its first letter

explanation.surface: Tom must arrange a small bull to be offered up.
explanation.walkthrough: A tomcat is a HE-CAT; OM is the British Order of Merit; 'a little' gives the first letter of bull.
explanation.definitionFit: A hecatomb was a great public sacrifice in ancient Greece, originally of a hundred oxen.

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous early car, so a model gives T
a rhymester is a writer of verse, a minor poet

explanation.surface: A word chosen for a poet who is a role model.
explanation.walkthrough: The Model T Ford gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimester is a period of three months, used as an academic term in some schools and universities.

clue.text: Hitler's first cat cavorting with mouse under his very nose

indicators.note: cavorting is leaping about, so the letters are thrown into a new order
first means only the opening letter of Hitler's is used

explanation.surface: Hitler's cat plays with a mouse right under his nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes H from Hitler's, and 'cavorting' rearranges H with CAT and MOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A moustache is hair grown on the upper lip, literally right under the nose, as with Hitler's famous one.

definitions.meaning: foul as in stinking or offensive
a row is a line, as of soldiers drawn up in ...

explanation.definitionFit: Rank means foul-smelling as an adjective, and a line of soldiers as a noun, matching row.

definitions.meaning: relish here is taste or liking, from the French word for taste
a painful condition affecting the joints, especially the big toe

explanation.definitionFit: Gout is borrowed from French for taste or relish, and in English names a painful inflammation of the joints.

indicators.note: explodes means the words blow apart and their letters land in a new order

parts.note: E, east, is one of the compass points

explanation.surface: The moment of peril is when the thing goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' gives E (east, a compass point), and 'explodes' rearranges DANGER with E; the whole clue also describes the bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A grenade is a small hand-thrown bomb, most dangerous at the moment it goes off.

clue.text: Six-footer takes test in three parts

definitions.text: Six-footer takes test in three parts

parts.words: Six-footer takes test in three parts
parts.note: a tall person sitting an exam seems meant, but the six feet are metrical feet, and the name breaks into three parts: six, a, and a measure

explanation.walkthrough: The name splits as HEX (Greek six), A, and METER (a measure or test), and a line in this metre has six feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A verse line of six metrical feet is a six-footer in the prosodic sense, the metre of Homer and Virgil.

clue.text: A refusal with little force can be soothing

parts.note: no is a refusal
a dyne is a tiny unit of force in physics

explanation.surface: Saying no gently can calm things down.
explanation.walkthrough: The dyne is a very small unit of force.
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne remedy relieves pain, so the adjective means soothing.

clue.text: Times review of an old theologian

annotationWithheld.why: Times review of an old theologian (7): ERAS (Times) gives the start, but no word of 'review of an' gives MUS; no parse found
annotationWithheld.clue: Times review of an old theologian

indicators.note: about means going around, so the idiot surrounds the number

parts.note: a twit is a fool
IL is 49 in Roman numerals, L for fifty less I for one

explanation.surface: A dull-witted fool of about forty-nine.
explanation.walkthrough: IL for 49 is a loose crossword use of Roman numerals (strictly XLIX); 'about' has the fool wrapped round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Twilit means lit by twilight, so dim.

parts.note: read as two words, the best person who owes money would be the most creditworthy debtor; read whole, it is one who gives

explanation.definitionFit: One who bestows is a giver or donor, and the word splits whimsically into best ower, a model debtor.

clue.text: He trod the boards formerly in Lancashire

parts.note: old means of former times
a ham is an actor, especially an overacting one, who treads the boards of the stage

explanation.surface: Someone who used to act on stage in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trod the boards' means acted on stage; a HAM is a poor actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldham is a mill town in Lancashire, northwest England, so it is found in that county.

parts.note: patients are the ill, those who are sick

explanation.surface: A physician prescribes a workout for his patients.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a repeated training exercise, as in fire drill or army drill.

clue.text: Cops nearly failed through not keeping awake

indicators.note: failed suggests the words have gone wrong and broken up, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Police almost fell short because they kept nodding off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failed' rearranges the ten letters of COPS NEARLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcolepsy is a disorder causing sudden attacks of sleep, a failure to stay awake.

indicators.note: took means the answer is taken from inside the run of letters in William Booth

explanation.surface: The Salvation Army founder played a role in the hexameter clue.
explanation.walkthrough: William Booth founded the Salvation Army. 17 is HEXAMETER, a line made of metrical feet.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical foot, so it can be one of the parts that make up a line of verse such as 17.

annotationWithheld.why: They troubled Macmillan and Steven (6): EVENTS is STEVEN rearranged, but 'troubled' is both the anagram indicator and part of the definition 'They troubled Macmillan', so one word does two jobs

clue.text: He was known for an old windbag

definitions.text: He was known for an old windbag

parts.words: He was known for an old windbag
parts.note: a famous bore seems meant, but the windbag is the bag of winds handed to Odysseus in Greek myth by their keeper

explanation.walkthrough: In the Odyssey the keeper of the winds gave Odysseus the winds tied up in a leather bag.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god who ruled the winds is remembered for the bag of winds he gave Odysseus.
